stories.summary: Ajay tells of his college days when, as a 'callow immature youth,' he was spouting one limerick every ten minutes. The mathematician Meena Mahajan, a year senior at college, gave him the Marathi-style nickname 'Limya' — the equivalent of calling someone 'limerick boy.' Amit responds by revealing he is perhaps the only professional limerick writer in the world, having written a weekly limerick for the Sunday Times of India for years until it became 'too political.'
stories.insight: A small reminder that the bookish public-intellectual life often begins as silly play — limerick obsession at twenty becomes essay-craft at fifty. Take the play seriously.

stories.summary: A storage trader spends years in a boring, low-margin business — buying tomatoes, paying for cold storage, occasionally making tomato paste. Most years, the work is dull and barely profitable. But once in ten or twenty years, when the price of tomatoes briefly surges to infinity, the trader makes 'like a bandit' — and that one windfall pays for the decade of unsexy infrastructure-building. The Indian state, however, descends precisely in those windfall moments and confiscates the upside in the name of consumer protection.
stories.insight: Storage and speculation have an option-like, insurance-like character — the rare windfall is the entire economic case for the boring years. Kill the windfall and you destroy the supply of the service society needed in the first place.

stories.summary: To dramatise what an APMC feels like to a farmer, Amit imagines a parallel universe where columnists must, by law, sell their writing only at one Central Press Market Committee. Columnists would get a 'tiny little figure'; anyone wanting their work would pay a crazy markup; the writing market would die. The mismatch between the freedoms urban elites enjoy and the freedoms they deny farmers is the entire moral problem.
stories.insight: An empathy hack against ivory-tower paternalism — translate the constraint into your own profession and feel the outrage. The people most willing to deny others choice almost never apply that constraint to themselves.

stories.topic: Meeting Farmers Who Had Lived Hayek
stories.summary: Five or six years before recording, Barun Mitra took Amit to a meeting of farmer leaders from across Maharashtra near Nashik — many associated with Sharad Joshi's Shetkari Sanghatana. Amit went in carrying ideas of liberty he had absorbed from books — Hayek, Bastiat, frameworks. He came out shaken: every farmer leader he met had arrived at exactly his beliefs about the parasitic state, but had arrived there from lived experience, not from reading. (Out of that trip came his only Hindi episode of The Seen and the Unseen, with Gunvant Patil.)
stories.insight: First-principles libertarianism is not an elite import — it is what people figure out for themselves when the state has its boot on their neck. The condescension of saying 'farmers won't understand markets' is itself the disease.

stories.summary: After the Indian government banned BT (genetically modified) cotton on precautionary grounds, a group of Gujarati farmers obtained the seeds through the black market and planted them. In a year when bollworms catastrophically destroyed cotton crops across Gujarat, the BT plots flourished — so the government announced it would destroy the surviving crops as illegal. Sharad Joshi and the Shetkari Sanghatana mobilised farmers from across the country, marched to Gujarat and stood on the fields saying 'over our dead bodies,' then marched to Delhi with bales of cotton. The Vajpayee government relented, the ban was lifted, and within years over 90% of Indian cotton was BT — making India the world's largest cotton producer, surpassing China.
stories.insight: Farmers are not passive victims to be protected from technology by the state; they are entrepreneurs who will adopt what works, by guerrilla means if necessary. A genuine Gandhian satyagraha for the right to use a seed is one of independent India's great unsung freedom struggles.

stories.topic: The Climate-Change Argument for a Liquid Land Market
stories.summary: From his work at XKDR Forum, Ajay has come to believe the world will not hold back the rise in atmospheric CO2 — which means above the Vindhyas, Indian heat and water stress will become unliveable for traditional agriculture. The humane response is for households to sell northern land and move (south of the Vindhyas, perhaps out of agriculture entirely). But India's land market is so illiquid that sellers cannot exit at fair value and buyers cannot easily acquire, so households 'hug the land' as climate change grinds away their livelihoods.
stories.insight: Bad land policy locks people into vanishing futures. A liquid land market is not a luxury — it is climate adaptation. Mobility is mercy.

stories.topic: Sharad Joshi — The Civil Servant Who Became a Farmer
stories.summary: Born in 1935, educated in commerce at Sydenham, Sharad Joshi taught economics and statistics, then served as a civil servant in informatics at Bern and the UN between 1968 and 1977. In his early forties he chose to come back to India, bought 23 acres in a village called Ambethan in Pune district, and became a full-time farmer. From inside the experience, he diagnosed the problem precisely — that every farmer's misery traced back to state overreach — and built the Shetkari Sanghatana, drew lakhs to rallies, coined the phrase 'negative subsidy,' and in 1986 launched a women's wing (Shetkari Mahila Aghadi), once gathering two lakh women farmers in a single rally with no men.
stories.insight: Real public intellectuals close the gap between idea and ground. Joshi showed that liberal ideas can be mass politics — not by softening them, but by speaking them in the language of the people who already live their consequences.

recommendations.item: Down to Earth
recommendations.creator: Sharad Joshi
recommendations.context: A collection of Sharad Joshi's columns.
recommendations.reason: Joshi was a great thinker, a great mass-politician, and a serious public intellectual who put real work into his columns. To understand Indian agriculture from the worm's-eye view of a farmer-leader who actually lived it, this is the resource.

recommendations.item: Talking to an Empty Room
recommendations.creator: Sharad Joshi
recommendations.context: A collection of Joshi's speeches in the Rajya Sabha.
recommendations.reason: The title breaks Amit's heart — Joshi had great ideas the country desperately needed, and he was speaking them into a chamber that didn't care. A reminder of how much policy-quality knowledge gets wasted in Indian public life.

recommendations.item: The Wizard and the Prophet
recommendations.creator: Charles C. Mann
recommendations.context: A book about Norman Borlaug (the wizard, of the Green Revolution) and William Vogt (the prophet, of environmental limits).
recommendations.reason: The defining tension of the next twenty-five years of the food system: scientific-industrial intensification vs. sustainability. Sets up the question of how India goes from feeding 1.4 billion to a food system consistent with planetary and human health.

recommendations.item: The Price of Onions
recommendations.creator: Ashok Desai
recommendations.context: An old book of essays on the political economy of Indian food prices, anchored in the recurring onion-price drama.
recommendations.reason: Tomatoes today are exactly the onion story repeated — Desai's framing of the politics of food prices is timeless because the underlying interventions never change.

recommendations.item: The Mystery of Capital
recommendations.creator: Hernando de Soto
recommendations.context: The Peruvian economist's book on dead capital — assets people own but cannot legally use as collateral or transact freely.
recommendations.reason: Opened Amit's eyes to how much of what surrounds us — slum dwellings without title, agricultural land that can't change use, FSI-restricted plots — is 'dead capital,' worth a fraction of what working property rights would unlock.

recommendations.item: Why the Future Doesn't Need Us
recommendations.creator: Bill Joy
recommendations.context: Bill Joy's 2000 Wired essay warning about the runaway risks of nanotechnology, AI, and genetic engineering.
recommendations.reason: Ajay invokes it as the cautionary frame: editing DNA is harder than editing computer code, and we know how badly software fails. Approach with respect — neither ban nor blank cheque.

recommendations.item: The Tragedy of Our Farm Bills (Episode 211, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit's earlier deep-dive episode with Ajay on the 2020 farm bills.
recommendations.reason: The longer treatment of the same political-economy story this episode compresses.

recommendations.item: India's Agriculture Crisis (Episode 140, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand
recommendations.context: A broad survey of what's broken in Indian agriculture.
recommendations.reason: The episode where Barun Mitra pointed out that across 24 commodities for which MSPs are promised, only six actually receive them in practice — gives the empirical underbelly of the MSP critique.

recommendations.item: The State of Our Farmers (Episode 86, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Gunvant Patil
recommendations.context: Amit's only Hindi episode of The Seen and the Unseen, recorded after meeting Maharashtrian farmer leaders associated with the Shetkari Sanghatana.
recommendations.reason: The episode in which Amit first heard farmer-leaders articulate Hayekian ideas not from books but from lived experience — a 'masterpiece of illumination.'

recommendations.item: Futures Markets in Agriculture (Episode 12, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Shashidhar
recommendations.context: Amit's earlier conversation on why agricultural futures markets matter.
recommendations.reason: Demystifies futures markets as a basic tool for ordinary farmers, not arcane finance — the price discovered by speculators is a public good for everyone making sowing decisions.

recommendations.item: Entry and Exit in Agriculture (Episode 1, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pavan Srinath and Karthik Shashidhar
recommendations.context: The very first episode of The Seen and the Unseen, on scale and corporatisation in Indian agriculture.
recommendations.reason: Where Amit first encountered the argument that demanding every farmer simultaneously be a farmer and an entrepreneur is unfair — specialisation requires scale.

recommendations.item: The Right to Property (Episode 26, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Shruti Rajagopalan on how India's broken property rights regime hobbles agriculture and urbanisation.
recommendations.reason: Rajagopalan's exposition of the land-use-certificate scam — the same plot worth Rs 100 as farmland and Rs 4000 as developable land — is the deep dive behind the shorter version Amit gives here.

recommendations.item: India's Water Crisis (Episode 60, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Vishwanath S (zenrainman)
recommendations.context: A deep dive on groundwater depletion in India.
recommendations.reason: Connects the dots between MSPs for water-intensive crops, free farm electricity, bore wells, and the depletion of the water table — a textbook chain of bad incentives.

recommendations.item: Our FSI Problem (Episode 11, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Alex Tabarrok
recommendations.context: An episode on the absurdity of India's Floor Space Index restrictions on urban development.
recommendations.reason: Source of Tabarrok's striking line that 'in Bombay you reclaim the sea — you need to reclaim the sky' — extending Amit's argument that India is full of artificially dead capital.

recommendations.item: How I Reversed My Type 2 Diabetes (Episode 9, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Their earlier EIE episode arguing that cereals (rice, wheat, sugar) are at the root of the Indian diabetes epidemic.
recommendations.reason: The bitter twist on the MSP story — the government is subsidising the very cereals the same government's health system should be telling people to eat less of.

recommendations.item: The Incredible Insights of Bastiat and Hayek (Episode 6, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The earlier EIE episode on the price system as a carrier of information and incentives.
recommendations.reason: Foundational backstop for this episode's analysis of why interfering with food prices destroys the only mechanism that coordinates millions of independent decisions.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The EIE episode on freedom as the prerequisite for economic flourishing.
recommendations.reason: The companion piece to this one — the principle, of which agriculture is the case study.

recommendations.item: The Indian State Is the Greatest Enemy of the Indian Farmer
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on how state interventions, not markets, are what oppress Indian farmers.
recommendations.reason: The condensed written version of the argument running through this entire episode.

recommendations.item: We Must Save Our Farmers
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's piece in Pragati on the depth of the agrarian crisis.
recommendations.reason: Self-recommended along with his other agriculture writing as an entry point into the policy diagnosis.

recommendations.item: Farmers, Technology and Freedom of Choice: A Tale of Two Satyagrahas
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on the BT cotton and HTBT cotton movements as Gandhian-scale civil disobedience for technology.
recommendations.reason: The longer written version of the BT cotton satyagraha story he tells here, with the figures on adoption.

recommendations.item: What Happened to Global Food Prices?
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's column on global food-price dynamics.
recommendations.reason: Shows how the international market is the great buffer against domestic shortages — and why India's habit of banning imports and exports at whim destroys the very stabilisation it claims to seek.

recommendations.item: Economic Freedom in Agriculture
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's longer argument on how to free Indian agriculture from state controls.
recommendations.reason: Sets out the four-mechanism framework — futures, storage, domestic trade, international trade — that organises this episode.

recommendations.item: India: An Agricultural Trade Powerhouse
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's column on India's underappreciated strengths in agricultural trade.
recommendations.reason: Companion to the case for letting Indian farmers sell to the world — and importing freely when the country is short.

recommendations.item: Climate Change for Practical People
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay's framing of climate change as a problem of adaptation and policy reform rather than of moral exhortation.
recommendations.reason: The longer version of the climate-and-land-markets argument — why a liquid land market is climate adaptation.

recommendations.item: Rhyme and Reason
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: The archive of Amit's weekly limericks for the Times of India.
recommendations.reason: Self-referenced as evidence Amit was 'perhaps the only professional limerick writer in the world' — a small, charming taste of the limerick habit at Sunday-newspaper scale.

core_ideas.concept: The Price System as a Rationing Mechanism
core_ideas.explanation: Supply must equal demand at the moment of clearing — not because of magic, but because the price moves until enough buyers walk away. The less flexible buyer behaviour is, the bigger the price move has to be. Wheat and rice (cheap calories no one would skip) need huge price swings to ration; avocados (luxuries) need only small ones. Tomatoes in India sit at the inflexible end, which is why a 10% shortage produces a hundredfold price move from Rs 2 to Rs 200.
core_ideas.quote: The price system should be understood as a rationing mechanism.

core_ideas.explanation: If farmers naively look only at last season's price, a high tomato price triggers oversowing, which crashes the price, which triggers undersowing, which spikes it again — a permanent oscillation. The model needs three failures simultaneously: backward-looking expectations, fixed inputs, and no storage technology. In healthy economies these are solved by futures markets, flexible inputs, and storage businesses. India's tomato cycle exists because we have systematically broken all three solutions.
core_ideas.quote: Samuelson's cobweb model wants a certain kind of dysfunctionality.

core_ideas.concept: The Four Mechanisms That Stabilise a Food Market
core_ideas.explanation: (1) Futures markets — speculators publish a price that everyone freely uses to make sowing and storage decisions; the price is a public good. (2) Storage — cold storage, warehousing, and processing into puree, paste, dehydration that move food across time. (3) Domestic trade — moving surplus from one state to another. (4) International trade — the global market as an infinite buffer for both shortages and surpluses. The Indian state has crippled or banned all four.
core_ideas.quote: The price that the speculators make on the futures market is a public good.

core_ideas.concept: Storage as Service, Hoarding as Slur
core_ideas.explanation: Storage and speculation are intellectual, capital-intensive activities completely distinct from farming. The storage operator buys when food is cheap, locks it in cold storage at private risk and cost, and releases it when food is dear — depressing prices for consumers in the bad year. This is socially valuable insurance work, but Indian cinema and politics labelled it 'hoarding.' The Essential Commodities Act criminalises it, which is why India lacks the cold-storage and processing capacity that would dampen tomato volatility.
core_ideas.quote: This I call God's own work.

core_ideas.concept: The APMC Trap and Negative Subsidy
core_ideas.explanation: Indian farmers are legally required to sell only at their local Agricultural Produce Market Committee — a state-mandated monopsony where a small ring of licensed traders captures the bulk of the value chain. Sharad Joshi calculated that the wedge thus extracted from farmers (combined with export bans, MSP betrayals, and price suppression) far exceeds the visible 'subsidies' (free electricity, fertiliser). Farmers are not net subsidy recipients; they are net donors to the state. He called it the 'negative subsidy.'
core_ideas.quote: Marte tum bhi ho, marte hum bhi hai. Hum sasta bech ke marte hai, tum mehnga khareed ke marte ho.

core_ideas.concept: Land Use Certificates and Dead Capital
core_ideas.explanation: Indian farmers cannot easily convert agricultural land to non-agricultural use; only another farmer can buy it, so the market price is artificially depressed. The same plot can be worth Rs 100 as farmland and Rs 4000 once a land-use certificate flips it. So the standard scam is to acquire farmland cheap then use political contacts to flip the certificate. Meanwhile the genuine farmer is trapped — can't exit cleanly, can't capitalise the land for credit. Hernando de Soto's frame — 'dead capital' — applies to vast tracts of Indian land, slums, and FSI-suppressed urban plots.
core_ideas.quote: You can check out, but you can never leave.

core_ideas.concept: Subscale Farming Is Not a Lifestyle, It's a Failed Business
core_ideas.explanation: On one or two acres of land, farming is structurally unprofitable, technologically impoverished, and chronically dependent on a single local creditor-cum-input-seller-cum-buyer in a near-feudal arrangement. Romance about the family farm or about cooperatives doesn't fix subscale economics. The way out is land consolidation — twenty-, two-hundred-, two-thousand-acre farms run as businesses, with mechanisation and a real market for landless labourers (which is just labour, not a curse word). Land-leasing, land transactions, and the right to exit are prerequisites.
core_ideas.quote: It's a business, it's an entrepreneurial problem.

core_ideas.explanation: Minimum Support Prices began as good-intentioned price assurance for farmers in the 1960s. Their unintended effects include: (1) cereals received MSP, pulses didn't, so farmers shifted from pulses to cereals — starving the country of vegetarian protein for decades, (2) MSP for rice plus free farm electricity in arid Punjab caused groundwater collapse and the Delhi smog problem (rice stubble burning), (3) MSP-driven sugarcane and rice exports turn India into one of the world's largest virtual exporters of fresh water from a country that doesn't have any to spare. Robert Lucas called this kind of intervention one of the worst in economic history.
core_ideas.quote: India is one of the biggest exporters of water in the world.

core_ideas.explanation: Rich economies move people out of agriculture into manufacturing and services and out of villages into cities — that is what 'development' means at the structural level. The US has 2-4% of workers in agriculture; Europe single digits. By the cleaner CMIE-CPHS measure (primary income from agriculture), India is around 35% — eight to nine times the developed-country level. India had one great burst of structural transformation between 1991 and 2011; before and after, it has stalled. The persistence of subscale farming is the absence of structural transformation. Climate change is now coming for the people who never moved.
core_ideas.quote: The pace of transformation from rural to urban has been mild.

core_ideas.concept: Speculation as Insurance, Windfall as Premium
core_ideas.explanation: A storage operator's economics are option-like: dull, low-margin work most years, with the rare price spike paying for the entire decade. In healthy markets, this windfall premium is the entire reason anyone builds storage. The Indian state's habit of confiscating the windfall in the name of consumer protection (export bans, raid powers, price ceilings) systematically destroys the supply of the service. Same logic as vaccine manufacturers in a pandemic — destroy the upside and you destroy the capacity that would have saved the next bad year.
core_ideas.quote: It's an option-like character, it's an insurance-like character.

core_ideas.explanation: Resentment at the gap between farm-gate price (Rs 2) and consumer price (Rs 20) gets channelled into populist hatred of middlemen, who in India are often particular occupational castes and rich communities. Ajay's caution: the middlemen are not the disease. The disease is the lack of competition among middlemen — created by the state — which lets a small ring extract enormous rents. Hating the rent-takers without changing the rules just gives you a different rent-taker. Free entry would compress middleman margins automatically.
core_ideas.quote: What is at fault is not those individuals who are maximizing their own economic opportunities.

core_ideas.concept: Liquid Land Markets as Climate Adaptation
core_ideas.explanation: Above the Vindhyas, the combination of rising temperatures, water stress, and changing rainfall is making traditional agriculture unviable. The humane response is for households to sell their land and move — perhaps south of the Vindhyas, perhaps out of agriculture entirely. But India's land market is too illiquid for either side of that transaction to clear. So households 'hug the land,' staying with a livelihood climate change is destroying. Bad land policy is now also bad climate policy.
core_ideas.quote: The cognitive failure of households will then be to embrace the land.

core_ideas.explanation: Genetically modified crops have been used by farmers around the world for decades without identifiable harm. BT brinjal feeds Bangladesh; golden rice has prevented blindness from vitamin-A deficiency in the Philippines; BT cotton turned India into the world's largest cotton producer. The populist objection is largely funded by interests that lose if GMO succeeds (the pesticide lobby, alarmist NGOs). Caution about gene editing in the abstract is fine — Bill Joy's worry has merit — but the empirical record on GMO food crops is decisively positive. The precautionary principle taken too far stops all progress.
core_ideas.quote: If there is anything on which there is scientific consensus, it is this.

core_ideas.concept: The Power of Ideas in Public Policy
core_ideas.explanation: These bad agricultural interventions did not come from nowhere — they came from the top of a previous generation's agricultural-economics consensus. As Keynes observed, even the maddest practical men are usually the slaves of some defunct academic scribbler. The choke point on Indian policy is not corruption or politics; it is the absence of a new generation of paradigm-changing thinkers. Build the literature, change the climate of opinion, and policy follows.
core_ideas.quote: Madmen in frenzy are just stealing ideas from obsolete thinkers.

core_ideas.concept: Bharat Speaks Hayek Without Reading Hayek
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's eye-opening realisation at a Shetkari Sanghatana meeting near Nashik: every farmer leader he met held essentially the same beliefs about markets, freedom, and the parasitic state that he did, but had derived them from lived experience rather than from books. Liberal economic ideas are not an elite imposition on India; they are what people figure out for themselves when state controls have made their lives unliveable. The condescension that 'farmers won't understand markets' is itself the disease.
core_ideas.quote: They had not read Hayek. But they agreed with every word.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit's opening limerick for Ajay: 'My good friend Ajay sat in his chair / Reading YouTube comments in his head aglow, like a tomato. / The fulsome praise made his cheeks go.' (Ajay is 'tomato' for blushing at the comments.)
Amit on the great tomato shortage: 'Are you hiding tomatoes in your cheeks, or are you happy to see me?' — riffing on the famous Mae West line.
Amit on the 200-rupees-per-kg tomato drama: people flying into India from abroad were getting requests to fill their suitcases with tomatoes.
Ajay on the staid storage business that pays for itself one year in ten: 'This I call God's own work.'

Ajay blames Bengali cinema for India's storage policy: hoarding became a slur because of 'so many Bengali movies around hoarders' that the Indian state outlawed storage. Amit, half-Punjabi, declines to take the bait — 'we shall not refer to the other half.'

Amit's 'CPMC' thought experiment — imagining a world where columnists were legally forced to sell only to one Central Press Market Committee at one-tenth the going rate, to dramatise what an APMC feels like to a farmer.
Amit on the irony of land illiquidity and climate change: 'If the state won't allow our land markets to be liquid, maybe climate change will create liquid land markets.'

Amit's deflection of Ajay's recommendation requirements: 'You must recommend at least one book in every episode.' Ajay's defence: 'Books are very nerdy and I'm very nerdy. So I thought it'll be hajaar cool to go beyond books and talk about fun things — kefir and masala tea.'

Sharad Joshi's couplet, voiced by a farmer to a consumer: 'Marte tum bhi ho, marte hum bhi hai. Hum sasta bech ke marte hai, tum mehnga khareed ke marte ho.' ('You die my friend, and so do I. I sell my produce cheap and die, you pay so much that you die.') A negative-sum trap created by the APMC monopsony.

Sharad Joshi's central distinction between 'India' (the urban, English-speaking elite) and 'Bharat' (the rural, agricultural majority), with state policy systematically transferring wealth from Bharat to India.
John Maynard Keynes on the practical men of power being 'slaves of some defunct economist' — invoked by Ajay to argue that bad policy is downstream of bad ideas, not bad people.
Alex Tabarrok on Bombay: 'In Bombay you reclaim the sea. You need to reclaim the sky.' Tabarrok's case for vertical urban density against India's punishingly low FSI rules.

Hernando de Soto's 'dead capital' — assets people own but cannot fully use as collateral or transact freely, from The Mystery of Capital. Amit applies it to slums, FSI-restricted plots, and farmland trapped under land-use rules.
Bill Joy's 2000 Wired essay 'Why the Future Doesn't Need Us' — invoked as the cautionary balance to the GMO optimism, on the unique difficulties of editing DNA versus editing computer code.
B.S. Minhas — invoked by Ajay as the great Indian economist who helped persuade his generation that farmers are rational economic agents, not 'subhuman creatures who are unable to make decisions.'

Ashok Gulati on India as 'one of the biggest exporters of water in the world' — because rice and sugarcane are essentially virtual water exports, made profitable only by perverse MSP and free-electricity incentives.

Mrinal Pande, in Pragati's brainstorm symposium: 'Behind every crisis in India, there is a further layer which is a crisis of the women in it.' The insight that drove Sharad Joshi to launch the Shetkari Mahila Aghadi in 1986.
The 1986 Shetkari Mahila Aghadi rally with two lakh women farmers and no men — a now-mythic image of mass mobilisation in rural Maharashtra.

Robert Lucas (alluded to via the framing) on MSP-and-procurement as 'one of the world's worst policy interventions' — Re 1 raised in tax imposes about Rs 3 of social cost, then is used to subsidise rice and wheat that worsen public health, water tables, and Delhi air quality.
